newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai woes to worsen on Philippine peso fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai woes to worsen on Philippine peso fall.

text.p: Thailand's currency and short term economic problems could intensify following the Philippine peso's de facto devaluation last Friday, analysts said.

The peso's effective devaluation put renewed pressure on the recently floated Thai currency. The baht sank to a record 30.10/30.30 baht per dollar late on Friday against a central bank midrate of around 25.90 per dollar prior to the Thai action -- a de facto depreciation of around 15 percent.

A further weakening of the baht, which has been crawling lower since its July 2 float, could spell trouble for the equity market and severe pain for a number of Thai corporates with high dollar debts.

At 30 baht to the dollar the country's largest conglomerate Siam Cement Plc faces exchange losses of 9.9 billion baht ($330 million) this year on its $4 billion baht in unhedged foreign loans. Siam Cement's profits for 1996 were 6.787 billion baht.
The equity market, since rising 90 points in three trading sessions after the baht was floated, lost 28.54 points or 4.3 percent last week to close on Friday at 628.55.

With many offshore fund managers thinking the baht may yet weaken further, investors who entered the market last week are growing nervous and the prospects of foreign inflows will diminish until the currency is believed to have bottomed out, traders and analysts said.

"I just spent the last few days in Hong Kong seeing fund managers and my sense is a whole that most people are saying that you've got 10 percent downside on the currency because the baht is going to slide out to 32, so there are not many buyers," said Russell Kopp, head of research at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
Adding to weight the baht may weaken further in the short term are the $3 billion per month Thailand is estimated to need to pay off $35-40 billion dollars of short term foreign debt, analysts said.
The peso's effective devaluation also means Thailand's post baht flotation export advantage over comparable Philippine goods is likely to be eroded, analysts said.
That leaves the overall situation for the baht and the Thai economy in the short term highly uncertain, they said.

"I think it is very difficult to find a real value for the baht. For the next three months it's very difficult to predict the situation during this adjustment period," said Somchai Trairattanapiron, vice president at Sitca Investment and Securities.

On the positive side most houses were so underweight in Thai equities they missed out on a 130 point devaluation rally and fear they might fail to connect another bounce if funds suddenly flooded back in, analysts said.
"On fundamentals no one wants to own this market but the fundamentals got screwed last week and everyone is afraid of funds flowing in," said Kopp.
In the short term those funds would come in response to International Monetary Fund (IMF) involvement in the financial management of the country, analysts said.
The fund has been offering technical assistance to the Bank of Thailand but the signs are the Thai authorities would prefer Japanese government help.
Thailand's Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya will meet his Japanese counterpart for talks next week and may be seeking up to $20 billion in assistance, analysts said.
The commitment would help ease a liquidity squeeze which is moving from the ailing finance and securities sector and into the lower end of the banking chain, analysts said.
"The situation is very fluid and I'm telling my clients to stay out for the moment," said a senior trader at a European broker. ($1 = 29 baht)
